structure: papillae around the orbital opening of the inner chamber duct of the infrared receptor organ (accessory structure)
measurement: presence or absence of the papillae (absent: the duct opens as a simple preocular opening)
method: gross morphology of catalogued museum specimens (18 pitviper species examined; the Methods list 15 catalogued Crotalus durissus specimens (MZUSP 7308; CD 1813, 2344-2351, 2492, 2494-2495, 2497-2498) and do not state specimen sex); light, scanning and transmission electron microscopy were run on a subset of species that included Crotalus durissus, with the number of individuals not stated
conditions: collection specimens from MZUSP and the Universidad del Valle collections (wild-collected status and localities not stated); the paper reports the papillae present in all examined species of the Neotropical genera Bothriopsis, Bothrocophias, Bothropoides, Bothrops, Lachesis, Porthidium and Rhinocerophis, and absent in Agkistrodon piscivorus, Atropoides nummifer, Bothriechis schlegelii, Crotalus durissus and Ovophis okinavensis; the papillae are described as unknown in function and lacking the infrared-sensitive terminal nerve masses of the pit membrane; no measurements are given

value: largest scanning angle of the sonar beam between successive calls: 42 degrees real (51 degrees apparent)
method: free-flying wild bats recorded with a microphone array (successive call directions compared); single-microphone recordings in open space gave call amplitude differences between successive calls (mean 8.1 +/- 5.3 dB, up to 24 dB)
conditions: wild common pipistrelles in search flight at edge sites (forest road, farm, garden) in central France and in open space near Tubingen, Germany; number of bats not stated (abstract reports 33 flight sequences, Methods 32; calls analysed given as 725 in one place and 402 in another); sex not reported; the authors note that scanning angles in the abstract were often larger than the maximum angle measurable by the array, so 42 degrees is a floor set by the array, not the animals' maximum; sequences with irregular or no scanning movement were also recorded; successive calls pointing the same way score 0 degrees; pseudoreplication across individuals cannot be completely excluded (authors); this is emission behaviour of the call beam, not a hearing or detection threshold

value: resting-frequency (RF) echolocation call peak frequency varied from day to day, sometimes by more than 900 Hz, while the short constant frequency (SCF) communication calls stayed extremely constant
method: calls of pairs of bats recorded in an observation cage with an ultrasonic acquisition system over repeated days, January to September 2008; only calls emitted at rest analysed (RF calls, no Doppler shift compensation); day-to-day variation in peak frequency compared between RF and SCF calls
conditions: captive greater horseshoe bats, printed as Rhinolophus ferrumequinum tragatus, 8 bats analysed (6 males, 2 females), the only ones that produced SCFs among the 13 males and 7 females used in pairings, from a colony of 29 from Northern China housed in the bat facility at UCLA; the authors refer to their limited sample size of 8 bats; all bats combined: mean variation of RF peak frequency over the whole observation period 693.8 +/- 352.98 Hz (n = 1754 calls) against 245.0 +/- 78.19 Hz for SCF (n = 4275), about 35% of the RF variation (+/- most likely SD, not defined in the text); the study did not play back or mask sound, so feedback control is inferred from natural day-to-day variation, not tested; the authors note an observation period of under a week for some analyses is short; RF call peak frequencies before an SCF sequence did not differ significantly, and call durations always differed significantly between days for both call types

method: echolocation calls of hand-held captured bats recorded and the resting frequency compared among sites; frequency tested against climate and body-size predictors in a sensory-drive analysis (site means, one-way test F8,103 = 424.235, P < 0.001)
conditions: 112 adult wild Geoffroy's horseshoe bats captured at their roosts at sites in eastern and southern Africa (11 sites are named in the Methods; the F-test degrees of freedom, 8 and 103, imply 9 sites with 112 bats in the RF comparison); sex determined visually, number of each sex not read; neither body size nor sex had an effect on RF; the authors report climate (mean annual temperature) as the main predictor, but that RF was still higher than expected from body size, so sensory drive cannot explain the anomalously high frequencies of this species; emission frequency only, not hearing sensitivity

value: null: when played echolocation pulses of two foreign species with overlapping frequencies (Rca87 against Rbl87), bats discriminated habituation from test playback in only 3 of 10 trials, not different from the control
method: habituation-dishabituation playback of recorded Rhinolophus capensis and R. blasii echolocation pulses to R. clivosus in a sound-attenuating box, discrimination scored from video (attentive behaviour after the change of playback)
conditions: Experiment One: 12 male bats, 49 successful trials in all; wild-caught at De Hoop Guano Cave, then held in captivity at the University of Cape Town; Fisher exact test p > 0.05 against the control; in two of the four playback combinations involving foreign species (Rcl92-Rbl92, Fisher exact p < 0.0005; Rcl92-Rca87, p < 0.05) there were significantly more trials with discrimination than in the control; the other own-foreign pair, Rcl92-Rbl87, was not significant at the 95% level (p = 0.056; 6 of 8 trials discriminated), so this foreign-foreign pair is one of two non-significant combinations; for Rca87-Rbl87 attentive behaviour still lasted significantly longer in the test than at the end of habituation (Wilcoxon Z = 2.02, p < 0.05), though not significantly longer than in the control; bat order and playback order were randomised; Experiment Two (31 bats: 10 males, 21 females; 92 successful trials) found the longest attentive responses to changes in the CF component frequency (median 4.3 s), then duty cycle (3.9 s) and FM sweep rate (3.2 s), with no significant difference in response duration among the three tests; behavioural discrimination of playback, not a hearing threshold
